<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults with chronic joint pain often exhibit decreased mobility. Daily walking measures are being increasingly used in aging research as objective indicators of mobility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this study, we aimed to examine the effects of a 12-week hybrid exercise-based program on daily-life walking characteristics.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 59 community-dwelling older adults (aged ≥65 years) with mild to moderate knee and/or low back pain were randomized to either a hybrid exercise group or an educational control group. Daily-life walking was monitored using an ankle sensor. Daily observation data were collected within 2 planned 7-day windows. Primary parameters included activity volume and gait characteristics. Statistical analyses were conducted based on a modified intention-to-treat principle using linear mixed-effects models, with a per-protocol set used for sensitivity analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The mixed-effects analysis based on the modified intention-to-treat principle (n=52 participants; 696 observations) suggested an effect of the intervention on improving walking quality, particularly step length (β=2.39 cm;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.04; Hedges
                      <jats:italic>g</jats:italic>
                      =0.493), with a smaller effect with borderline statistical significance observed on improving walking speed (β=0.05 m/s;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.06; Hedges
                      <jats:italic>g</jats:italic>
                      =0.496). Cadence, daily distance, daily steps, active energy expenditure, and accumulated 3 or more metabolic equivalent of task activities showed no clear difference between the groups. In the per-protocol sensitivity analysis (n=44), the same directional pattern of improvement was observed for step length (β=1.95 cm;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.13; Hedges
                      <jats:italic>g</jats:italic>
                      =0.365) and walking speed (β=0.04 m/s;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.14; Hedges
                      <jats:italic>g</jats:italic>
                      =0.368); however, the estimates were imprecise.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 12-week hybrid exercise program may improve the quality of daily-life walking, with the clearest effect observed on step length. Given the attenuation after multiplicity-aware interpretation and in sensitivity analyses, these findings should be interpreted as suggestive rather than definitive.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Association Between a Hybrid Video-Guided Multicomponent Exercise Program With Staff Assistance and Free-Living Gait in Older Adults With Knee and Low Back Pain: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Controlled Trial

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Subjective cognitive decline (SCD) typically refers to self- or informant-reported decline in cognition despite the absence of objective impairment on standardized testing. Older adults with documented normal cognitive test performance provide a pragmatic anchor cohort for electronic health record (EHR)–based SCD phenotyping. However, cognitive concerns are primarily recorded in unstructured notes and are inconsistently documented, making it unclear how often and in whom concerns are captured in routine care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to operationalize EHR-based SCD phenotyping in an objectively normal-testing cohort using a large language model (LLM)–based natural language processing approach and to examine the frequency and clinical and sociodemographic correlates of cognitive concern documentation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted an EHR-based observational study of patients aged 65 years or older with a first normal cognitive test recorded in EHR flowsheets between January 2019 and April 2024 in a large health care system. We developed and iteratively refined a 2-stage LLM-based natural language processing pipeline to identify documented cognitive concerns in unstructured notes during the 12 months prior to the index date, and evaluated performance against manual review. We quantified the frequency of documented concerns within this normal-testing cohort and used multivariable logistic regression to assess associations with sociodemographic factors (age, marital status, insurance, and neighborhood Area Deprivation Index), sequentially adjusting for clinical comorbidities and relevant medications.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Among 15,750 older adults with normal cognitive test scores, 13.8% (n=2175) had at least 1 documented cognitive concern in the prior year, captured in 1.2% (7394/605,177) of notes. On manual validation, the 2-stage pipeline (Med42-v2-8B screening followed by GPT-4o confirmation) achieved a sensitivity of 0.957, positive predictive value of 0.935, specificity of 0.985, and
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score of 0.945 for cognitive concern identification. Documentation was more likely in older individuals, those with commercial (vs Medicare) insurance, and those with neurological and psychiatric conditions. In fully adjusted models, Parkinson disease (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 5.29, 95% CI 3.60‐7.77), traumatic brain injury (aOR 4.63, 95% CI 3.15‐6.81), stroke or transient ischemic attack (aOR 3.46, 95% CI 3.15‐4.18), epilepsy (aOR 2.52, 95% CI 1.83‐3.49), depression (aOR 1.54, 95% CI 1.36‐1.75), and excessive alcohol use (aOR 1.48, 95% CI 1.06‐2.06) were among the strongest correlates of cognitive concern documentation. In contrast, obesity (aOR 0.73, 95% CI 0.65‐0.82), hyperlipidemia (aOR 0.59, 95% CI 0.51‐0.67), and residence in more deprived neighborhoods (higher Area Deprivation Index) were associated with lower odds of documented cognitive concerns.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 2-stage LLM pipeline enabled accurate identification of documented cognitive concerns consistent with SCD among older adults with normal cognitive testing. Documentation was uncommon and selectively captured by clinical and sociodemographic factors, with implications for equity and the validity of EHR-based phenotypes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Large Language Model–Based Identification of Subjective Cognitive Decline in Electronic Health Records Among Older Adults With Normal Cognitive Testing: Retrospective Cohort Study

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Falls are a major cause of morbidity among older adults, yet fall risk may begin to emerge during midlife. Physical performance measures may identify early functional vulnerability associated with later-life health outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined whether midlife gait speed and muscle performance were associated with recurrent falls later in life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study was a secondary analysis of prospectively collected data from the Midlife in the United States (MIDUS) cohort. Independent adults (n=309) aged 45 to 64 years at wave 2 (2004-2009) who completed physical performance assessments were followed to wave 3 (2013-2021). Baseline measures included gait speed from a 50-foot walk test, grip strength, sit-to-stand time, and calculated lower-extremity power. The primary analysis examined associations between baseline physical performance and recurrent falls at follow-up (≥2 falls in the previous 12 months). A sensitivity analysis repeated the primary models but was restricted to participants without a baseline history of recurrent falls.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>At follow-up, 20.4% (63/309) of participants reported recurrent falls. Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls (odds ratio 1.43, 95% CI 1.05-1.95; P=.02), whereas muscle performance measures were not associated with falls in the primary analysis. The association between slower gait speed and recurrent falls remained significant in the sensitivity analysis. Over follow-up, muscle performance declined, whereas gait speed remained stable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Slower midlife gait speed was associated with higher odds of recurrent falls, suggesting that fall vulnerability may be detectable as early as midlife. Given the exploratory nature of this study, further studies are warranted to confirm these findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Associations of Midlife Gait Speed and Muscle Performance With Falls in Later Life: Secondary Analysis of the MIDUS Cohort

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intrinsic capacity (IC) is increasingly used to conceptualize healthy aging. However, evidence on socio-demographic correlates in IC among Hispanic older adults in the United States remains limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed data from a nationally sampled cohort from the 2022 Health and Retirement Study, including Hispanic adults aged ≥60 years. IC was constructed from five domains. Multiple linear regression models examined associations between socio-demographic factors and IC, with stratified analyses by gender, community of residence, and place of birth.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The sample included 749 participants (60.08% female; 89.05% urban residents; 63.02% foreign-born), with a mean IC score of 6.49 (SD = 1.67). In the overall sample, being male, married/partnered, having a household income above $28,034, and being physically active were positively associated with IC, whereas having two or more chronic diseases was negatively associated with IC (all p &lt; 0.05). Stratified analyses showed that physical activity was positively associated with IC among females, urban residents, foreign-born participants, and US-born participants, while having two or more chronic diseases was negatively associated with IC across most subgroups. Among the interactions examined, only the association between physical activity and IC differed significantly by gender (p &lt; 0.05).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Physical activity and chronic disease burden were important correlates of IC among Hispanic older adults, with some subgroup-specific patterns observed across gender, residential community, and place of birth. These findings highlight the importance of considering demographic and contextual factors when promoting healthy aging among Hispanic older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Intrinsic capacity among Hispanic older adults in the United States: Sociodemographic correlates and subgroup analyses

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Financial fraud is a common and consequential threat among older adults, with estimated prevalence rates ranging from 4% to 17% annually. Although cognitive decline has been widely studied as a risk factor, less is known about behavioral characteristics that may predict changes in scam susceptibility. In the present study, we examined whether blind giving predicted trajectories of scam susceptibility across a two-year period and whether this association differed as a function of age.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>One hundred and sixteen cognitively unimpaired older adults (aged 51 to 83; 72% female) completed a behavioral economic measure of blind giving at baseline and a self-report measure of scam susceptibility annually across three visits.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Linear mixed-effects models revealed a significant interaction between time, blind giving, and age (p = .022), such that greater baseline blind giving was associated with increasing scam susceptibility over time among relatively older participants, whereas scam susceptibility remained stable across levels of blind giving among relatively younger participants. Blind giving was not associated with scam susceptibility at baseline (p = .515), and the longitudinal association persisted after separately adjusting for global cognition, socioeconomic status, and race (all ps ≤ .026).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Greater blind giving predicted longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility over a two-year period, with this pattern observed specifically in advanced age. These findings suggest that prosocial tendencies may become maladaptive in later life, underscoring the importance of identifying at-risk individuals to inform prevention efforts in aging populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Blind giving predicts longitudinal increases in scam susceptibility in later life

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Enthusiasm for artificial intelligence (AI) that continuously infers emotion promises to change how care systems identify older adults at risk of loneliness. We use AI-driven loneliness detection to mean systems that infer loneliness, or a proxy for it, from sensed data rather than from a person’s answer, rendering the inference as a score or category used in care; they range from facial and vocal emotion recognition to behavioral risk prediction from everyday activity data. Engineering feasibility, more than any social-gerontological understanding of loneliness, has driven this agenda, and little attention has gone to how older adults in different cultural contexts wish to be known and supported. Because such detection is not yet in routine use in Taiwan, this Forum article adopts an anticipatory-governance stance, examining before deployment a trajectory that policy makes plausible. Anchored in Taiwan’s ageing society and long-term care system, it argues that culturally responsive design should begin with older adults’ own meanings, relational obligations, and expectations of privacy and autonomy, not with the sensors. It identifies three tensions for social gerontology: the reframing of a relational experience as an individual biometric deficit; the risk that algorithms read culturally patterned emotional restraint as noise; and the slippage from care toward surveillance once risk indices enter routine care workflows. Taking seriously the case for technological augmentation of scarce care resources, the article proposes principles for a socially accountable approach and a research agenda on how older adults negotiate being sensed, scored, and ‘connected.’</jats:p>
title: Being Sensed, Scored, and ‘Connected’: A Social-Gerontological Critique of AI-Driven Loneliness Detection for Older Adults in Taiwan

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) applications are increasingly used to support independent living and care for older adults, particularly those in vulnerable situations. Yet, how vulnerability is constructed when AI enters later-life care remains poorly theorized. Existing approaches to vulnerability in old age inadequately address AI-related risks, structural conditions, exposure pathways, and life course disadvantages. Using a theory-synthesis approach, this article proposes “vulnerability intersections” as an integrative framework for how vulnerability is constructed, enacted, and negotiated in AI-assisted care for older adults. The framework extends existing sociotechnical accounts by conceptualizing vulnerability as taking four overlapping forms: anticipatory, opaque, routinized, and normative. It locates vulnerability factors at the micro level of older adults’ lives, the meso level of care organizations and technology providers, and the macro level of political-economic and regulatory arrangements, with life-course accumulation spanning all three. It also proposes three exposure pathways through which vulnerability factors become consequential: AI-mediated information and representations of aging; AI-powered care organization and delivery; and AI-configured power, participation, and social relations. The framework shifts attention away from viewing older adults as inherently vulnerable toward examining the sociotechnical arrangements under which vulnerability is anticipated, classified, distributed, and negotiated when AI enters care.</jats:p>
title: Vulnerability Intersections: An Integrative Conceptual Framework for Understanding Vulnerability in AI-Assisted Care for Older Adults

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Little is known about how older adults experience their return home after wartime displacement, particularly when home and community are altered or remain insecure. This longitudinal qualitative study examined continuity and change across the displacement–return transition.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twelve participants (aged 65–92), previously interviewed during displacement (T1), were re-interviewed after returning home (T2) using a qualitative descriptive approach with thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Three themes emerged: (1) the unsettled return, involving altered security, unfamiliarity within the home, and disrupted community life; (2) continuity of social relationships and activities after return; and (3) shifts in life perspective and self-perception. These themes describe the shared dimensions of post-return experience, whereas the complementary diachronic analysis examined how these dimensions changed and combined across T1 and T2. A diachronic analysis identified four return trajectories: functioning but incomplete; ambivalent or gradual return requiring active reorganization; return supported by communal and social continuity and use of personal resources; and ongoing erosion and unresolved damage.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings demonstrate that return is not restoration but a reconfiguration of person-environment fit, place identity, belonging, and security in later life. For older adults, this transition involved rebuilding environmental familiarity, security, belonging, and agency rather than simply resuming pre-displacement life. The study highlights social infrastructure as critical for post-return adaptation, underscoring the need for policies recognizing the return process as a significant transition requiring continued communal support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Ambivalent return: Older adults’ homecoming after wartime displacement

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The experience of grandparenthood holds the potential for novel and engaging social interactions and activities, which may protect against cognitive decline. The present study outlines how individuals believe grandparenthood has impacted their cognitive abilities in late life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We asked 127 grandparents (87 grandmothers and 40 grandfathers) how they thought grandparenthood had impacted their mental ability (memory, concentration, and cognitive ability). An exploratory thematic analysis utilizing a codebook approach was conducted on the participant responses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Analysis revealed four major themes among the responses: “grandparenthood as a continuous experience that promotes healthy cognitive functioning”, “shifting perspectives”, “limited interaction”, and “the negative impacts of grandparenthood.”</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A majority of grandparents expressed the belief that interacting with their grandchildren is beneficial to their cognition. However, some participants qualified grandparenthood as a stressful experience that has negatively impacted their cognitive health. These findings support previous literature showing both cognitive benefits associated with grandparental caregiving and negative cognitive outcomes that may result from the stress of caregiving.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: ‘Keeping me sharp”: Self-perceived effects of grandparenthood on cognition: An exploratory thematic analysis

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults who identify as lesbian, gay, or bisexual (LGB) may be at increased risk of elder abuse (EA) due to unique risk factors; however, research in healthcare settings has been limited by the lack of data on sexual orientation. Since 2022, the Veterans Health Administration (VHA) has collected self-reported sexual orientation for all patients. The objective of this chart review study was to use newly available electronic health record (EHR) data to explore the documented experiences of older LGB adults identified with EA concerns.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We randomly sampled 100 of 201 Veterans aged ≥60 years with an outpatient visit between 10/2022-9/2023 who identified as LGB and had a social work visit for possible abuse/neglect. We conducted protocolized chart reviews of clinical notes within ±180 days of the social work visit for 23 LGB patients, with EHR documentation confirming EA, to describe key characteristics and documented EA experiences.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 23 EA cases in LGB Veterans, 8 (35%) had cognitive impairment, 8 (35%) reported a history of child maltreatment, and 7 (30%) reported military sexual trauma. Veterans’ sexual orientation was sometimes noted to contribute to past abuse experiences; however, the relationship between sexual orientation and EA or EA care processes was rarely documented by clinicians.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings highlight important considerations for sexual orientation minority patients experiencing EA, including opportunities to examine both contributors to EA risk among older LGB patients and to address LGB-specific care needs for this population in future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Characterizing lesbian, gay, and bisexual patients’ experiences with elder abuse: A chart review study

<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examined whether the latent structure of social determinants of health (SDOH) differs by nativity and how they relate to health outcomes in later life.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using 2016–2018 HRS data, exploratory factor analyses by nativity were conducted, followed by nativity-stratified regressions linking SDOH factors to health outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Four comparable factors emerged in both groups: neighborhood environment, interpersonal stressors, socioeconomic resources, and family support. Loading patterns showed modest nativity differences: among immigrants, social isolation aligned more strongly with family support than socioeconomic resources and perceived discrimination loaded weakly on interpersonal stressors. Interpersonal stressors were associated with poorer mental and cognitive health in both groups; socioeconomic resources were associated with better health outcomes but more weakly among immigrants. Associations of neighborhood environment and family support with health varied by nativity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings indicate substantial commonality in SDOH structures alongside suggestive nativity-related differences, warranting replication in larger immigrant samples.</jats:p>

records.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined psychological correlates of quality of life (QoL) among older adults in a Latin American context, focussing on the roles of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress. Hierarchical multiple regression analyses were used to examine the incremental contribution of sociodemographic factors, three dimensions of ageism, self-disgust, and psychological distress to QoL among 272 Colombian older adults (mean age = 68.40, SD = 6.80). Findings indicated that interpersonal experiences of ageism, but not exposure to ageist messages or self-ageism, were associated with poorer QoL. Higher self-disgust and psychological distress were independently associated with lower QoL and formed part of a significant indirect association between interpersonal ageism and QoL. These findings suggest that quality of life in later adulthood is associated not only with structural and sociodemographic conditions, but also with psychological processes through which age-related stigma may be experienced and internalised. Interventions that reduce interpersonal ageism while promoting self-acceptance and more positive views of ageing may represent promising avenues for supporting wellbeing and quality of life in older adults.</jats:p>

We compared the narratives of young and older participants about a TV series when recalled to a young or older listener. records.abstract: <jats:p>Ageism is widespread and intensified during the COVID-19 pandemic, with resource shortages contributing to healthcare guidelines that systematically deprioritised older adults. Whilst the ethical considerations of these guidelines are well documented, perceptions of age and ageism in healthcare allocation remain underexplored. Using thematic analysis, three themes were developed: (1) age determines health, (2) age determines the value of life, and (3) age determines acceptance of death. records.abstract: <jats:p>In contemporary dementia care, behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia (BPSD) are often understood as expressions of the person's intentions or needs. This paper examines the limits of understanding BPSD as “expressions of intention” in severe Alzheimer's disease. It argues that while desires may still be preserved, the formation and maintenance of beliefs—an essential constituent of intentions in the standard desire–belief model—are likely to be severely compromised. As a result, many behavioral and perceptual symptoms closely related to basic activities of daily living cannot be adequately explained within an intention-based framework. As a complementary framework to existing dementia care theories, this paper proposes a reconceptualization of BPSD as arising from the interaction between embodied procedural memory and environmental affordances. Many BPSD are better understood not as expressions of intention, but as the outcome of situational and non-selective reactivation of fragments of relatively preserved procedural memory in response to the structure of the immediate environment. This reconceptualization extends the focus of care practice beyond the interpretation of the presumed meanings or intentions underlying BPSD and highlights the importance of modifying care environments in ways that appropriately support or constrain the reactivation of procedural memory.</jats:p>
title: Rethinking Behavioral and Psychological Symptoms of Dementia in Severe Alzheimer's Disease: From Intentional Explanation to an Ecological, Body–Environment Framework

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Intrinsic capacity (IC) is defined by the World Health Organization as the sum of an individual’s physical and mental abilities that support health and well-being. While well validated internationally, it has not been operationalized and validated in a nationally representative US cohort.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from 5,834 community-dwelling older adults from Round 12 (2022) of the National Health and Aging Trends Study (NHATS) survey, we identified measures related to IC domains (cognition, locomotion, vitality, psychological, sensory). We performed exploratory factor analysis (EFA), omega hierarchical reliability testing, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) using bi-factor and second-order structures. We also constructed the Integrated Care for Older People (ICOPE) screening tool. Descriptive statistics and regression models were used to examine the associations of IC and ICOPE scores with demographic and health characteristics. Age- and sex-specific reference centile curves were developed using empirical percentiles.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>EFA consistently supported a six-factor structure (vision and hearing were separate). Omega hierarchical analysis supported a strong general factor (ω = 0.92; ωₕ=0.72), and the bi-factor model demonstrated excellent fit. IC and ICOPE scores showed strong correlation (r = 0.71). Higher IC scores were associated with younger age, higher level of education, and income. Prevalence of comorbidities, frailty, ADL and IADL disability increased from the highest to the lowest IC and ICOPE quartiles. Reference centile curves demonstrated progressive age-related decline, with females showing lower IC scores than males.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We demonstrate IC operationalization in a nationally representative U.S. cohort and provide the first US-specific reference centile curves. The findings provide a foundation for future IC research in the US.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Intrinsic Capacity in a Nationally Representative US Population

                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Deprescribing fall risk–increasing drugs (FRIDs) is essential for reducing polypharmacy and falls in older adults, yet randomized controlled trials (RCTs) face unique implementation challenges. The DeFRID study is an ongoing multi-center RCT evaluating an ARMOR-based deprescribing intervention versus usual care in adults aged ≥60 years prescribed FRIDs. The objectives of this review are threefold: (1) to describe practical challenges encountered during a multi-center deprescribing RCT in India; (2) to propose a conceptual framework for categorizing these barriers; and (3) to contextualize DeFRID's experience within the broader deprescribing research landscape.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a narrative review with systematic scoping elements, synthesizing global RCT evidence from PubMed, OpenAlex, and Google Scholar (inception–December 2025) with DeFRID process evaluation data. DeFRID barriers and facilitators were identified via mixed-methods (clinician KAP questionnaire and qualitative interviews), team meetings, retention logs, and Phase II RCT implementation data, thematically categorized, then compared with global RCT challenges.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>DeFRID implementation revealed four challenge categories: ethical–clinical difficulties establishing equipoise for FRID withdrawal; operational barriers to recruitment and retention; methodological complexities in fall outcome ascertainment; and context-specific constraints unique to the Indian LMIC setting—limited deprescribing guidelines, polypharmacy normalization, fragmented care coordination, and hierarchical decision-making. Global RCTs revealed substantial implementation challenges: low clinician adherence, short follow-up periods, restrictive eligibility excluding frail or cognitively impaired older adults, and resource-intensive interventions limiting scalability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Deprescribing FRIDs in older adults is impeded by ethical, operational, methodological, and provider-patient challenges, necessitating multilevel strategies integrating training, shared decision-making, context-specific guidelines, and stakeholder engagement for scalable implementation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Deprescribing Fall Risk–Increasing Drugs in Older Adults: Implementation Challenges and a Conceptual Framework from the DeFRID Trial and Global Evidence

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prevailing scientific evidence suggests that extreme heat poses a substantial threat to the health and well-being of older adults in the Sunbelt cities of the United States. However, prior research has not adequately addressed the specific socio-demographic, health-related vulnerabilities, and coping-strategic factors influencing heat stress among older urban populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Informed by the Socio-Ecological Model, this study adopts a retrospective cohort study design to investigate the predictors and experiences of heat stress among older adults. Data from older adults in Los Angeles, Houston, and Phoenix were analyzed using thematic and multiple binary logistic regression analyses.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results reveal that much older adults (aged 80 +) were less likely to experience heat stress compared to their relatively younger counterparts. Also, marital status, income, respiratory diseases, physical activity, taking cool showers, and city of residence were significantly associated with a higher risk of suffering heat stress. The qualitative results uncovered individual-level behavioural adjustment as an effective coping mechanism during extreme heat events.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These results underscore the complex interplay of behavioral, socio-demographic, and health-related factors influencing heat stress among older adults. The study recommends that urban health strategies prioritize these demographics, enhancing support systems and coping mechanisms to reduce vulnerability to heat stress among older urban populations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Heat stress and coping strategies among older adults in three Sunbelt cities in the United States

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Age-related increases in chronic systemic inflammation are strong predictors of morbidity and mortality in high income countries, but evidence is lacking from lower- and middle-income settings where infectious diseases are more prevalent and rates of overweight and obesity are relatively low. Here we evaluate two complementary measures of chronic inflammation—plasma C-reactive protein (CRP) and a DNA methylation–based surrogate (DNAm-CRP)—measured at baseline as predictors of physical capacity, cognitive function, and cardiometabolic disease seven years later among women in the Philippines (N = 953; 43-75 years at follow-up). Levels of CRP and DNAm-CRP were not strongly associated with age. Both measures predicted subsequent declines in physical and functional capacity, increased incidence of diabetes and hypertension, and poorer cognitive performance, after adjustment for baseline status and other covariates. DNAm-CRP performed comparably to CRP, and was robust to variation in white blood cell composition and acute infectious symptoms at the time of sampling. These findings demonstrate that chronic inflammation is associated with multiple dimensions of aging in a lower-middle income setting, and highlights the utility of inflammatory biomarkers as scalable tools for global aging research.</jats:p>
title: Chronic inflammation and multiple dimensions of aging among women in the Philippines

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Frailty is a major determinant of disability and adverse outcomes in older adults. The Planetary Health Diet (PHD), a plant-based dietary pattern promoting environmental sustainability, has been associated with lower mortality and reduced chronic disease risk. We examined the association between adherence to the Planetary Health Diet Index (PHDI) and frailty over time using repeated frailty assessments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data came from two cohorts of community-dwelling older adults: Seniors-ENRICA-1 (2008-2015; ≥60 years; n = 3,289) and Seniors-ENRICA-2 (2015-2023; ≥65 years; n = 3,273). Baseline diet was assessed using a validated diet history, and adherence to the PHD was assessed using the PHDI (0-140), based on 15 food groups. Frailty was defined by the Fried phenotype (≥3 criteria of exhaustion, low physical activity, slow gait, muscle weakness, unintentional weight loss). Generalized estimating equation (GEE) models estimated odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) for frailty across PHDI tertiles, adjusting for sociodemographic, lifestyle, and clinical factors.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher PHDI adherence was consistently associated with lower odds of frailty over time. Comparing highest vs. lowest tertiles, multivariable-adjusted ORs (95% CI) were 0.62 (0.42, 0.92) in Seniors-ENRICA-1, 0.40 (0.24, 0.65) in Seniors-ENRICA-2 and 0.52 (0.38, 0.70) in the pooled analyses. Higher PHDI adherence was primarily associated with lower odds of low physical activity, while vegetables and fruits showed the strongest independent associations among individual PHDI components.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Greater PHDI adherence is associated with lower odds of frailty in Spanish older adults, supporting the potential role of sustainable, plant-based dietary patterns for healthy ageing.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Planetary Health Diet Adherence and Frailty in Older Adults: Evidence from the Seniors-ENRICA Cohorts

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults constitute a growing and heterogeneous proportion of intensive care unit (ICU) admissions, and early risk stratification in this group remains difficult. The lactate-to-albumin ratio (LAR) is a composite biomarker that combines a marker of acute metabolic derangement with one of physiological reserve, and has shown prognostic value in several critical care settings. Its performance in geriatric ICU patients, and specifically whether it adds information to established severity scores, has not been established.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted a retrospective, single-centre cohort study of consecutive patients aged ≥ 65 years admitted to the mixed medical–surgical ICU of a tertiary referral hospital in Türkiye between January 2024 and July 2025. LAR was calculated as serum lactate (mmol/L) divided by serum albumin (g/dL), from samples obtained within the first 6 h of ICU admission. The primary outcome was all-cause 28-day mortality. Discrimination was assessed by area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), and curves were compared using the DeLong test. Multivariable logistic regression assessed whether LAR was independently associated with mortality after adjustment for age, sex, Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS), SOFA, APACHE II and C-reactive protein (CRP).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Of 296 screened admissions, 294 were analysed; 98 patients (33.3%) died within 28 days. Non-survivors had higher admission LAR than survivors [1.37 (IQR 0.84–2.50) vs. 0.62 (IQR 0.46–0.99),
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001]. LAR discriminated 28-day mortality with an AUC of 0.793 (95% CI 0.740–0.846), significantly better than serum lactate alone (AUC 0.746; ΔAUC 0.047, 95% CI 0.021–0.074,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.0005) and serum albumin alone (AUC 0.656; ΔAUC 0.137, 95% CI 0.061–0.213,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.0004). APACHE II discriminated considerably better than LAR (AUC 0.924, 95% CI 0.893–0.955; ΔAUC 0.131, 95% CI 0.080–0.181,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). Adding LAR to APACHE II did not significantly improve discrimination (AUC 0.929 vs. 0.924; ΔAUC 0.006, 95% CI −0.0001 to 0.0115,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.055; likelihood ratio test
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.098). On univariable analysis LAR was strongly associated with mortality (OR 2.17, 95% CI 1.63–2.88,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001), but after full adjustment this association was no longer statistically significant (adjusted OR 1.29, 95% CI 1.00–1.66,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.052). APACHE II (adjusted OR 1.36, 95% CI 1.21–1.52,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001) and CRP (adjusted OR 1.06 per 10 mg/L, 95% CI 1.01–1.11,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.015) remained independently associated with mortality.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In critically ill older adults, admission LAR discriminates 28-day mortality better than either of its components alone and is strongly associated with mortality on unadjusted analysis. However, it did not add significant discriminatory information to the APACHE II score, and it was not independently associated with mortality after adjustment for illness severity. LAR may be useful as a rapidly available early indicator where a full severity score is not yet computable, but on these data it does not complement APACHE II.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Admission lactate-to-albumin ratio in critically ill older adults: superior to its individual components but not additive to APACHE II — a retrospective cohort study

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Malnutrition is a significant problem affecting the prognosis of elderly patients with heart failure. The objective of this study is to evaluate the nutritional status of geriatric patients suffering from heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF ≤ 40%) and to compare the effectiveness of the Mini Nutritional Assessment (MNA), Mini Nutritional Assessment-Short Form( MNA-SF), Subjective Global Assessment (SGA), and Controlling Nutritional Status (CONUT) malnutrition screening tools.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>One hundred thirty-eight patients aged 65 and over with heart failure were included in this study conducted at a tertiary care center. All participants were evaluated using the MNA, MNA-SF, SGA and CONUT score. Demographic data, clinical parameters, and laboratory findings were recorded.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The prevalence of malnutrition was found to be 16.7% according to MNA, 17.4% according to SGA, and 13.0% according to CONUT score. A significant correlation was found between all three assessment tools (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Malnutrition is a common problem in geriatric heart failure patients, requiring routine screening. All three assessment tools showed good correlation, suggesting their reliability in clinical practice. The MNA can be recommended as an initial screening tool, while SGA provides detailed assessment, and CONUT offers objective parameters. <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>After stroke, families take long-term responsibility for rehabilitation and care, and family resilience is an important measure of family adaptation. Predicting later family resilience from information collected early during hospitalization may help assess family support needs and plan follow-up care. This study aimed to develop and conduct a preliminary external validation of a model for predicting family resilience 6 months after stroke in older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We used a prospective two-cohort design. The development and independent external validation analyses included 310 and 102 older adults with stroke, respectively. Data were collected at baseline (T0), 1 month (T1), and 6 months after stroke (T2). Using 23 candidate predictors measured early during hospitalization (T0), we developed a least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) linear regression model to predict the continuous score on the shortened Chinese version of the Family Resilience Assessment Scale (FRAS-C) at 6 months (T2). The model was internally validated using repeated nested 10-fold cross-validation and bootstrap resampling, and the final model was applied directly to the independent external cohort. Performance was assessed using the coefficient of determination (R²), root mean square error (RMSE), and calibration measures and compared with the baseline FRAS-C-only model.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The final model included five predictors: baseline family resilience, self-care ability, social support, caregiver sex, and caregiver burden. In repeated nested cross-validation, the model yielded an R² of 0.555 (95% CI 0.499–0.603) and an RMSE of 2.959. In the external validation cohort, the R² was 0.409 (95% CI 0.269–0.508), the RMSE was 3.516, and the calibration slope was 1.165 (95% CI 0.897–1.429). Compared with the baseline FRAS-C-only model, the full model increased R² by 0.238 and reduced RMSE by 0.649 points in external validation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The model, which included baseline family resilience, patient functional status, and family caregiving characteristics, predicted family resilience at 6 months and added predictive information beyond baseline family resilience alone. It retained predictive performance in the independent external cohort and may be used to support family assessment early during hospitalization and follow-up planning after discharge.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Development and external validation of a model for predicting family resilience 6 months after stroke in older adults: a prospective cohort study

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Falls among older adults are a major public health concern and are associated with recurrent falls, functional decline, fear of falling, and reduced quality of life. Older adults presenting to emergency departments (EDs) following a fall are often discharged directly home despite ongoing rehabilitation and support needs. Although person-centred approaches are recommended in international guidelines, less is known about older adults’ and relatives’ experiences following an ED visit for a fall. This study aimed to describe older adults’ and their relatives’ experiences of a fall, including the ED visit and the transition back home.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative study design was used, involving semi-structured interviews with older adults aged 75 years and older and their relatives. Participants had attended the ED following a fall but were discharged without hospital admission. Seventeen participants (11 older adults and 6 relatives) were recruited. Data were analysed using qualitative content analysis according to Graneheim and Lundman.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The analysis generated one overarching theme,
                      <jats:italic>Sustaining agency through recovery across care and everyday life</jats:italic>
                      , which reflected how older adults and their relatives sought to manage daily life following a fall. Both groups described addressing immediate care needs while simultaneously adapting to longer-term changes in everyday life. Participants described difficulties navigating healthcare services to access follow-up care and rehabilitation, contributing to feelings of insecurity, financial strain, and increased responsibility. A persistent fear of falling affected daily activities and required adaptations and new roles for both older adults and their relatives. Despite these challenges, many participants demonstrated resilience and an ability to manage daily life following injury. Individual coping strategies and support from relatives were described as central to managing everyday life and healthcare contacts.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults discharged home after a fall may benefit from coordinated, person-centred follow- up that supports rehabilitation, recovery, and fall prevention. Despite variation in support needs, participants described a common need for clearer guidance and improved support structures, while also demonstrating considerable resilience and capacity for self-management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults with heart failure face significant symptoms and psychosocial burdens that routine cardiology care might overlook. We assessed whether Edmonton Symptom Assessment System (ESAS) and Integrated Palliative Care Outcome Scale (IPOS) scores can predict 12-month mortality and improve risk discrimination beyond clinical covariates in a hospital cohort from a low-resource setting.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We conducted an observational cohort study at the National Geriatric Hospital (Vietnam). Inpatients aged 60 years or older with chronic heart failure who met the eligibility criteria were approached in the order of admission (January 2021-December 2022), and ESAS (9 items, each scored 0–10) and IPOS (17 items) were completed within 48 h of admission by trained ward nurse-researchers. Vital status at 12 months was determined through medical records and structured follow-up calls. Cox proportional hazards models evaluated associations with mortality, adjusting for age, sex, heart-failure classification, New York Heart Association (NYHA) class, comorbidities, and financial strain. Primary analyses used predefined categorical cutoffs (ESAS > 30; IPOS ≥ 20). Discrimination was further assessed with Harrell’s C-index and the 12-month area under the curve (AUC), and model fit was compared using Akaike and Bayesian information criteria. Calibration was also examined using a logistic analogue (Hosmer–Lemeshow).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Of 327 screened patients, 304 were enrolled (mean age 71.9 ± 8.8 years; 52% men); 65 deaths (21.4%) occurred within 12 months. ESAS and IPOS were strongly correlated, but there was no multicollinearity. High symptom burden (ESAS > 30) independently predicted mortality (adjusted hazard ratio [aHR] 2.27; 95%CI 1.20–4.28), while high palliative-care needs (IPOS ≥ 20) were not associated (aHR: 1.04; 95%CI 0.47–2.30). Kaplan–Meier curves across ESAS–IPOS strata diverged. Including categorical patient-reported measures in the clinical model modestly improved discrimination and fit: Harrell’s C increased from 0.671 to 0.697 and 12-month AUC from 0.700 to 0.718 (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.034), with acceptable calibration and lower information criteria.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In hospitalized older adults with heart failure, a nurse-administered ESAS identified patients at independently higher 12-month mortality risk. IPOS, though clinically informative for care planning, added little prognostic information once symptom severity was considered. Brief, nurse-led symptom screening offers a feasible approach to risk stratification in resource-limited settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:title>Trial registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Osteoporosis is a major cause of morbidity and fractures among older adults, contributing substantially to disability, hospitalization, and mortality. This cross-sectional study investigated the associations of depressive symptoms and functional status with bone mineral density (BMD) and osteoporosis in hospitalized older adults.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed 1,048 hospitalized patients aged ≥ 70 years who underwent dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Depressive symptoms (GDS-15) and functional status (Barthel Index) were extracted from routine geriatric assessments. Group comparisons, multivariable linear regression, and logistic regression analyses were performed after adjustment for demographic, clinical, and endocrine covariates.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Lower Barthel Index scores and higher depressive symptom burden were independently associated with lower hip BMD, whereas associations with lumbar spine BMD were less consistent. Although statistically significant, the observed effect sizes were modest. The multivariable model explained a moderate proportion of BMD variability (adjusted R² = 0.22).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Functional and psychological characteristics were independently associated with bone mineral density in hospitalized older adults. Given the cross-sectional design, causal relationships cannot be established. These findings support the potential value of incorporating comprehensive geriatric assessment into osteoporosis evaluation to improve identification of older adults at increased fracture risk.</jats:p>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>As populations age globally, mental health remains a frequently neglected aspect of healthy ageing. Older adults face biological, psychological, and social challenges that heighten their risk of mental health problems, yet professional service utilization remains low. In India, this treatment gap is worsened by limited mental health literacy, stigma, and socio-cultural barriers. This study assessed mental health literacy and help-seeking behaviour among older adults in Mysuru, examined their association, and explored barriers and facilitators influencing professional help-seeking.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An explanatory sequential mixed-methods design was used. A community-based cross-sectional survey was conducted among 232 older adults (aged ≥ 60 years) selected through multistage stratified sampling from rural and urban Mysuru Taluk, Karnataka. Mental health literacy was measured using the Mental Health Literacy Scale (MHLS) and help-seeking behaviour using the Attitudes Toward Seeking Professional Psychological Help Scale (ATSPPH). Non-parametric tests and Spearman’s correlation were applied. Eight in-depth interviews followed, analyzed using Braun and Clarke’s thematic analysis and Lewin’s Force Field Analysis framework.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Participants had a median MHLS score of 105 (IQR 12), representing a substantial proportion of the maximum possible score of 160, yet only 7.8% had sought professional help in the preceding 12 months, with most turning first to family or friends. A significant negative correlation existed between mental health literacy and help-seeking attitudes (ρ = -0.262,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001). Education and family structure significantly influenced both outcomes. Five qualitative themes emerged: understanding of mental health, experiences of emotional distress, help-seeking and coping, barriers to care, and facilitators of support. Key barriers included stigma, emotional suppression, financial constraints, and misattribution of distress to normal ageing, while family support, awareness, and accessible services were key facilitators.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Despite a comparatively favourable median mental health literacy score, professional help-seeking among older adults in Mysuru remains limited. Targeted awareness interventions, stigma reduction strategies, and strengthened community-based mental health services are needed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Not applicable.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Mental health literacy and help-seeking behaviour among older adults in Mysuru, India: a mixed methods study

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Strengthening empowerment plays a pivotal role in supporting family caregivers of older adults with dementia. This study explored the comprehensive caregiving experiences of both family caregivers and dementia care professionals to identify and describe the components of family empowerment within the Korean context.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A qualitative study was conducted using semi-structured focus group interviews (FGIs). Participants included 14 family caregivers (3 groups) and 5 Dementia care professionals (1 group). Psychological Empowerment Model (PEM) served as the theoretical framework to understand the dimensions of empowerment. The specific components of empowerment in Korean family caregivers of older adults with dementia were analyzed using qualitative thematic analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Seven main themes and 14 sub-themes were identified as components of family empowerment. The main themes included: (1) Reconstructing the caregiving situation and awareness; (2) Acquiring dementia information through experiential means; (3) Satisfaction with doing my best in caregiving; (4) Balance between self-care and family care; (5) Securing and utilizing dementia-related resources; (6) Reflections of caregiving experiences; and (7) New roles and relationships created through caregiving.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings of the study elucidate that family empowerment of family caregivers of older adults with dementia is a multidimensional construct: it is established through the cognitive process of reconstructing caregiving perceptions, emotional fulfillment derived from the stability of the caregiving process, behavioral practices of balancing self-care with family care, and relational reinforcement gained through newly established roles. Future efforts should establish sustainable support systems through education, resource linkage, and emotional support. Additionally, we propose the development of empowerment intervention programs and measurement tools based on these identified components.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical trial number</jats:title>

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Older adults’ participation and intersectoral collaboration are central to the development of age-friendly environments. While previous research has emphasised the importance of these principles, less is known about how they are understood and enacted by societal actors in practice. This creates a need to explore societal actors’ perceptions of both intersectoral collaboration and older adults’ participation in the development of age-friendly environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study had a participatory qualitative design. Data were collected through a World Café involving 19 societal actors in a Swedish municipal context. Participants represented several societal sectors relevant to age-friendly environments, including welfare, care, public health, governance, social sustainability, urban planning,mobility, civil society, and voluntary engagement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings showed that participants perceived intersectoral collaboration as requiring shared societal responsibility across multiple sectors, while responsibility risked becoming unclear when no actor had an explicit mandate to coordinate, prioritise and act. Intersectoral collaboration was viewed as a way of sharing resources, yet also as vulnerable when it relied mainly on personal relationships and informal networks rather than organisationally embedded structures. Similarly, older adults’ participation was highly valued when developing age-friendly initiatives, but participants questioned whether existing participation channels adequately reflect the diversity of older adults’ experiences and needs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Age-friendly work requires shared responsibility across societal actors, supported by clear coordination. Personal relationships and informal networks should be recognised as valuable for enabling collaboration, but they need to be complemented by formal structures to ensure sustainability over time. Moreover, greater efforts to reach seldom-heard older adults are needed. Doing so may contribute to more nuanced and age-friendly initiatives that better reflect the diverse needs of the older population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Societal actors’ perceptions of intersectoral collaboration and the participation of older adults in the development of age-friendly environments

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      After a hospital stay, older patients are at increased risk of health complications that may lead to readmission to hospital or premature death. Globally, numerous interventions have been applied to enhance transitional care for older patients, but the evidence base remains inconclusive. One form of a transitional care intervention is the Swedish primary health care
                      <jats:italic>Safe homecoming</jats:italic>
                      intervention, a time-limited, interprofessional and tailored home health care intervention designed to prevent avoidable complications and readmissions following hospital discharge. The effects of
                      <jats:italic>Safe homecoming</jats:italic>
                      have not yet been scientifically evaluated. The present study aimed to assess the association between the interprofessional
                      <jats:italic>Safe</jats:italic>
                      <jats:italic>h</jats:italic>
                      <jats:italic>omecoming</jats:italic>
                      intervention and the risk of death or readmission.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We conducted a retrospective propensity score-matched cohort study in Örebro County, Sweden, using administrative and medical-record data from 2013 to 2020. The source cohort comprised 38,338 patients aged 75 years or older who had been admitted to hospital for at least one day. We included 128 patients who received the interprofessional
                      <jats:italic>Safe homecoming</jats:italic>
                      intervention at a single primary health care centre between 1 November 2016 and 31 May 2019 and 512 propensity score-matched controls from across the county receiving standard care.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The mean age was 85.5 years, and 60.9% of patients in both groups were women. At 90 days, the cumulative incidence of first hospital readmission was 20.3% in the intervention group and 33.6% among controls (Gray’s test
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.005). In the competing-risk analysis, the Fine-Gray subdistribution hazard ratio was 0.57 (95% CI 0.37–0.86;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.008). The corresponding cause-specific Cox model yielded an HR of 0.55 (95% CI 0.36–0.84;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.005). At 365 days, the Fine-Gray estimate was 0.79 (95% CI 0.59–1.05;
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       = 0.098). Mortality estimates favoured the intervention group numerically but were imprecise, with confidence intervals including the null at all evaluated follow-up times.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      <jats:italic>The Safe Homecoming</jats:italic>
                      intervention was associated with a lower risk of first hospital readmission at 90 days, whereas there was no clear evidence of an association with mortality or longer-term readmission. Given the observational design, small intervention sample, potential residual confounding and evaluation of multiple follow-up time points, these findings should be considered exploratory and require confirmation in larger prospective studies.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
title: Safe homecoming intervention after hospital discharge: a retrospective cohort study of mortality and readmission among patients 75 years or older in Sweden

records.abstract: <jats:p>Objectives: Episodic memory trajectories vary substantially between individuals in the second half of life: some maintain high levels of performance into their 80s, whereas others experience marked declines as early as their 50s. Identifying factors that help explain this heterogeneity is critical for understanding cognitive aging. Drawing on the resource substitution hypothesis and the Openness–Fluid–Crystallized–Intelligence (OFCI) model, this preregistered study examined whether the Big Five personality traits and their interactions with socioeconomic status (SES) predict individual differences in episodic memory trajectories, testing also potential non-linear associations. We expected higher openness and lower neuroticism to be associated with better memory levels and slower decline, with stronger effects at lower levels of SES. Methods: We analyzed data from 57,947 individuals aged 50 and older (M = 67.78, SD = 9.03) who participated in at least two waves (7, 8, or 9) of the Survey of Health, Ageing, and Retirement in Europe (SHARE). Multilevel growth models were used to estimate associations between personality and episodic memory levels and 5-year change, and whether SES (i.e., education, income, and wealth) moderated these associations. Results: Consistent with the OFCI model and the resource substitution hypothesis, higher openness was associated with better episodic memory levels, particularly among individuals with lower wealth. Higher neuroticism and lower conscientiousness were linked to poorer episodic memory levels, but only among less wealthy individuals. Higher extraversion was associated with better memory levels overall, and individuals at the extremes of extraversion exhibited somewhat flatter declines compared to those with moderate levels. Except for extraversion, there was little evidence for non-linear associations or for associations with 5-year change in episodic memory. Conclusion: Our findings underscore the relevance of wealth as an important socioeconomic resource for cognitive health beyond income and education, particularly in old age, when income is typically reduced. Overall, the results support modest concurrent associations between personality, SES, and episodic memory levels, but provide hardly any evidence for longitudinal effects. More frequent and longer-term longitudinal assessments are needed to clarify potential effects on cognitive aging.</jats:p>
title: Socioeconomic Differences in the Association Between the Big Five Personality Traits and Episodic Memory Trajectories in Midlife and Old Age
